summary.text: For \(n=2,3,4\), expressing a number and its reversal modulo \(3^n\mid81\) through their digit sum \(S\) and weighted digit sums gives \(3^n\mid S(9\ell-7)\); coprimality and the digit bounds force \(S=3^n\), \(\ell=3^{n-2}\), and every digit to be 9, while direct divisibility shows this all-nines number is admissible. For \(n\ge5\), repeating the palindromic block \(29799999792\) exactly \(3^{n-5}\) times gives a shorter self-reversing multiple of \(3^n\): the block supplies \(3^5\), and grouping the associated geometric sum in triples supplies the remaining power of 3.

full_proof.text:
Let \(\operatorname{rev}(m)\) denote the integer obtained by reversing the usual base-10 digit string of \(m\), with any zeros that become initial zeros discarded. For a positive integer \(d\), let
\[
 a(d)=d\min\{k\ge 1:d\mid \operatorname{rev}(kd)\},
\]
whenever this set is nonempty. Thus \(a(d)\) is the least positive multiple of \(d\) whose reversal is also divisible by \(d\). All the values considered below have an explicit admissible multiple, so the alternative value \(0\) in the definition of the sequence never arises.

We prove that, for every \(n\ge2\),
\[
 a(3^n)=10^{3^{n-2}}-1
 \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
 n\in\{2,3,4\}.
\]

We first establish the digit argument that handles \(2\le n\le4\).

Put
\[
 q=3^n,\qquad L=3^{n-2}.
\]
Since \(n\ge2\),
\[
 q=9L.
\]
Since also \(n\le4\), \(q\mid81\).

Consider any positive integer \(M<10^L\) such that both \(M\) and \(\operatorname{rev}(M)\) are divisible by \(q\). Write the decimal digits of \(M\), from least significant to most significant, as
\[
 D=(d_0,d_1,\ldots,d_{r-1}).
\]
Thus
\[
 M=\sum_{j=0}^{r-1}d_j10^j,
\]
where \(0\le d_j\le9\), and \(d_{r-1}\ne0\). Because \(M<10^L\), we have \(1\le r\le L\).

Define
\[
 S=\sum_{j=0}^{r-1}d_j,
 \qquad
 W=\sum_{j=0}^{r-1}j d_j.
\]
For the reversed digit list define similarly
\[
 W'=\sum_{j=0}^{r-1}j d_{r-1-j}.
\]
The elementary identity
\[
 W+W'+S=rS
\]
follows because a fixed digit \(d_j\) has coefficient \(j\) in \(W\), coefficient \(r-1-j\) in \(W'\), and coefficient \(1\) in \(S\), for total coefficient \(r\).

Modulo any divisor of \(81\), the binomial expansion gives
\[
 10^j=(1+9)^j\equiv 1+9j,

after all terms involving \(9^2=81\) are discarded. Consequently,
\[
 M\equiv S+9W\pmod q.
\]
Reversing the digit list does not change its digit sum, so likewise
\[
 \operatorname{rev}(M)\equiv S+9W'\pmod q.
\]
Both integers are divisible by \(q\). Adding the two congruences and using \(W+W'=rS-S\), we obtain
\[
 0\equiv 2S+9(W+W')
   =2S+9(rS-S)
   =S(9r-7)\pmod q.
\]
Now
\[
 9r-7\equiv-1\pmod3,
\]
so \(9r-7\) is relatively prime to every power of \(3\), in particular to \(q=3^n\). We may therefore cancel this factor and conclude
\[
 q\mid S.
\]

The digit sum is positive, because \(M>0\), and it satisfies
\[
 0<S\le9r\le9L=q.
\]
As a positive multiple of \(q\) no larger than \(q\), it must be exactly \(q\). Hence equality holds throughout:
\[
 S=q=9L,
 \qquad r=L.
\]
There are \(L\) digits, each at most \(9\), and their sum is \(9L\). Therefore every digit is \(9\). It follows that
\[
 M=\underbrace{99\cdots9}_{L\text{ digits}}=10^L-1.
\]
We have thus proved the following key conclusion:

> If \(2\le n\le4\), \(0<M<10^{3^{n-2}}\), and both \(M\) and its decimal reversal are divisible by \(3^n\), then
> \[
> M=10^{3^{n-2}}-1.
> \]

We now apply this conclusion to the three small exponents. Let
\[
 R_n=10^{3^{n-2}}-1.
\]
For \(n=2,3,4\), these numbers and their quotients by \(3^n\) are
\[
\begin{array}{c|c|c|c}
 n&3^{n-2}&R_n&R_n/3^n\\ \hline
 2&1&9&1\\
 3&3&999&37\\
 4&9&999999999&12345679.
\end{array}
\]
Thus \(3^n\mid R_n\) in all three cases. Moreover, each \(R_n\) consists entirely of nines, so \(\operatorname{rev}(R_n)=R_n\). Hence \(R_n\) is an admissible multiple and
\[
 a(3^n)\le R_n.
\]
In particular,
\[
 0<a(3^n)<10^{3^{n-2}}.
\]
By the definition of \(a\), the number \(a(3^n)\) itself is divisible by \(3^n\), and its reversal is also divisible by \(3^n\). Applying the key conclusion with \(M=a(3^n)\) gives
\[
 a(3^n)=R_n=10^{3^{n-2}}-1
\]
for \(n=2,3,4\).

It remains to show that the asserted equality fails for every \(n\ge5\). We do this by constructing an admissible palindrome strictly smaller than the all-nines number.

Let the 11-digit block be
\[
 B=29799999792.
\]
Its decimal digit string is a palindrome. A direct division gives
\[
 B=243\cdot122633744=3^5\cdot122633744,
\]
so \(3^5\mid B\).

Fix \(n\ge5\), and put
\[
 k=3^{n-5},\qquad x=10^{11}.
\]
Form the integer whose decimal expansion consists of \(k\) consecutive copies of the block \(29799999792\):
\[
 M=B\sum_{i=0}^{k-1}x^i.
\]
There is no ambiguity from leading or trailing zeros, since every digit of the block is nonzero. Because the block is palindromic and all the repeated blocks are identical, the entire \(11k\)-digit string is a palindrome. Thus
\[
 \operatorname{rev}(M)=M.
\]

We next prove that the geometric sum contributes the remaining factor \(3^{n-5}\). More generally, for every \(m\ge0\), define
\[
 G_m=\sum_{i=0}^{3^m-1}x^i.
\]
We claim
\[
 3^m\mid G_m.
\]
This follows by induction on \(m\). For \(m=0\), \(G_0=1\). For the induction step, write \(N=3^m\). Splitting a geometric sum of length \(3N\) into three blocks of length \(N\) gives
\[
 \sum_{i=0}^{3N-1}x^i
 =\left(\sum_{i=0}^{N-1}x^i\right)
   \left(x^{2N}+x^N+1\right).
\]
Since \(x=10^{11}\equiv1\pmod3\), the second factor satisfies
\[
 x^{2N}+x^N+1\equiv1+1+1\equiv0\pmod3.
\]
By the induction hypothesis the first factor is divisible by \(3^m\), and the second is divisible by \(3\); their product is therefore divisible by \(3^{m+1}\). This proves the claim.

Taking \(m=n-5\), we find
\[
 3^{n-5}\mid \sum_{i=0}^{k-1}x^i.
\]
Combining this with \(3^5\mid B\) yields
\[
 3^n=3^5 3^{n-5}\mid M.
\]
Since \(M\) is its own reversal, both \(M\) and \(\operatorname{rev}(M)\) are divisible by \(3^n\). Thus \(M\) is an admissible multiple for the definition of \(a(3^n)\).

We must compare its size with the proposed all-nines value. The number \(M\) has exactly \(11k\) decimal digits, so
\[
 M<10^{11k}.
\]
On the other hand,
\[
 3^{n-2}=3^3 3^{n-5}=27k.
\]
Since \(k>0\),
\[
 11k<27k=3^{n-2}.
\]
In particular, as these exponents are integers, \(11k\le 3^{n-2}-1\), and hence
\[
 M<10^{11k}
 \le 10^{3^{n-2}-1}
 <10^{3^{n-2}}-1.
\]
The final strict inequality is immediate because, for a positive integer \(N\),
\[
 10^N-1-10^{N-1}=9\cdot10^{N-1}-1>0.
\]
Therefore
\[
 M<10^{3^{n-2}}-1.
\]

As \(M\) is a positive multiple of \(3^n\), write \(M=t3^n\) with \(t\ge1\). Its reversal is divisible by \(3^n\), so \(t\) is one of the multipliers over which the minimum defining \(a(3^n)\) is taken. Consequently,
\[
 a(3^n)\le M<10^{3^{n-2}}-1.
\]
Thus equality with \(10^{3^{n-2}}-1\) is impossible for every \(n\ge5\).

Finally, if \(n\ge2\) and \(n\notin\{2,3,4\}\), then necessarily \(n\ge5\), so the preceding construction proves failure of the equality. Conversely, the digit argument proved the equality for each of \(n=2,3,4\). Hence, for every integer \(n\ge2\),
\[
 a(3^n)=10^{3^{n-2}}-1
 \quad\text{if and only if}\quad
 n\in\{2,3,4\}.
\]
